17129-the-missing-link:
Edward Dyson's 1922 novel centers on Nicholas Crips, called Nickie the Kid, a smooth talker who lives by wits on the edge of honest work and crime. His healing mixture opens the tale, and his circle of beats, sharpers, and soft marks gives the book its comic edge. Dyson paints Crips as bony, pale, and quick with a tale of sickness when a tale pays.

The humor comes from cons, near misses, and the gap between Crips' fine talk and his thin deeds. Set in Australian low life of its day, the novel mixes slang, satire, and caper plot. Readers who like rogues with charm and no shame will enjoy watching Nickie talk his way in and out of trouble.
21015-the-adventures-of-jimmy-skunk:
Peter Rabbit watches Jimmy Skunk vanish into an old barrel on a hill in Thornton Burgess's tale. The Imp of Mischief whispers at once in Peter's long ears, Burgess warns. Jimmy, once started, will not keep still unless made to, all agree.

The Adventures of Jimmy Skunk, from 1918, joins Burgess's vast bedtime story world. Reddy Fox, Peter Rabbit, and the Green Forest crew fill its small wars. Each scrape teaches real skunk lore beneath the fun and talk. Burgess wrote to make children love wild neighbours, and Jimmy's calm, smelly defence still wins that case.
21412-the-tale-of-bobby-bobolink:
Bobby Bobolink arrives in Pleasant Valley in Arthur Scott Bailey's Tale of Bobby Bobolink, a 1920 Sleepy-Time Tale. On May Day the feathered folk stop, look, and listen for the friend all await. Bobby is a singing bird of the meadows, proud of his song.

Chapters follow his greetings, his singing for a mate, and the house in the meadow. Johnnie Green, the farmer's boy, breaks in more than once, and Bobby must fool him. Mr Crow, Mr Catbird, and Timothy Turtle add fun and friction. Bailey's short tales give young readers a whole small world of field and swamp folk.
21845-the-tale-of-peter-mink:
Peter Mink has no home and a very long neck, and both facts shape this 1916 children's tale by Arthur Scott Bailey. Peter has no home because he does not want one; he sleeps wherever he happens to find a snug place. His clothes wear out fast from squeezing through small holes and cracks. In Pleasant Valley, everyone knows his shifting ways.

The chapters set Peter to sawing wood, passing the hat, and helping Jimmy Rabbit, whom he pulls out of the mud. A garden party, a circus parade, and a duck pond fill out his adventures. Bailey writes animal life as village comedy for young readers. Peter's bad temper and good turns make him a full little character in fur.
22876-the-link:
A starship slides toward its berth in The Link, a piece of science fiction. Other vessels tower around the berth in ring after ring, their bright spires aimed at the sky. Then the view blots out as grapples pull the vessel into the slot from which it rose days before.

Arrival is only the start. Stories named for a link usually promise a connection that changes everything, between worlds, minds, or times. This one builds its future from harbor routine in space, ships handled like liners at a dock. The method keeps the strange scene credible. Readers of classic magazine science fiction will recognize the manner, economical, visual, and more interested in the working future than in speeches about it.
23210-missing-link:
Missing Link is a work of science fiction set aboard a starship. Its central figure is a heavy planet native who feels uneasy on Gienah III. That world's gravity runs at only seven-eighths of Earth's standard, and the difference nags at him as he works.

On the bridge, he checks the control console, the chronometer, and a big glowing map of their position. Surgical scars on his neck, where tiny communications gear was set in, itch badly. The tale builds its future from such details: altered bodies, ship routine, and a man far from the heavy world that made him.
24005-but-i-don-t-think:
Randall Garrett's But, I Don't Think opens with a quotation from The Idle Worshipers by R. Phillip Dachboden. A physician, a painter, and a philosopher debate a religion with human sacrifice as an integral part, and the philosopher asks, with irritation, whether the victim might like it that way.

The story proper begins as the great merchantship Naipor settles tens of thousands of tons into her landing cradle on Viornis, gently as an egg into an egg crate. Space Captain Humbolt Reed orders High Lieutenant Blyke to bring the Guesser to his office at once. Garrett's tale is a spacefaring argument about freedom, slavery, and what thinking men think they know.
24246-greener-than-you-think:
Ward Moore wrote this novel, published by William Sloane Associates in New York in 1947, in a first edition. Its chapters run from Albert Weener Begins and Consequences of a Discovery through Man Triumphant in two parts, a South Pacific sailing discovery, and Mr. Weener Sees It Through. A note warns that neither the vegetation nor the people are entirely fictitious, yet no person pictured is the reader.

With one exception, Moore adds: the reader, whatever the country or station, is Albert Weener, as Moore himself is Albert Weener. The narrator once dreamed of writing a book to ease weary minds of the day's cares. Readers get a wry, unsettling tale of an ordinary man and a discovery that grows beyond him.
25095-joe-strong-the-boy-fish-or-marvelo:
Vance Barnum's Joe Strong, the Boy Fish, subtitled Marvelous Doings in a Big Tank, is a boys' circus adventure from the Whitman series about the young performer Joe Strong. The story opens at a packed circus, with bands playing, elephants trumpeting, and Joe preparing his acrobatic and trapeze turns.

Trouble follows quickly: a savage lion escapes its cage, and Joe must help keep the show going while the beast is loose near the grounds. A water act with a dog named Toto adds to the excitement. The book delivers exactly what its title promises, fast action, circus color, and a hero who keeps his nerve.
25523-old-junk:
H. M. Tomlinson selects travel and chance stories from his writings in periodicals between January 1907 and April 1918, arranged in order of time. He dedicates the book to C. H. G. H., a companion on much of what it describes, killed in action in Artois in August 1918.

Chapters run from the African coast and the call of the sea through old junk, bed-books and night-lights, the pit mouth, and the voyage of the Mona. Tomlinson writes as a watcher and wanderer, finding meaning in derelicts, lascars, and extra hands aboard ship.
2648-george-cruikshank:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote this essay on George Cruikshank, reprinted from the Westminster Review of June 1840. Thackeray opens on ingratitude, a charge laid against every inhabitant of a wicked world, and on men borne through trouble like swimmers in a crowd.

Cruikshank's etchings, crowded with rogues, dandies, and drunkards, get a critic who loves their energy and moral bite. Thackeray judges the artist as a historian of low life and high folly alike. The essay remains a lively tribute, and a reminder of how much Victorian England learned about itself from pictures.
27425-major-frank:
A. L. G. Bosboom-Toussaint wrote this Dutch novel, translated by James Akeroyd and published by T. Fisher Unwin in London in 1885. It opens with a letter from Sir Leopold van Zonshoven at The Hague in March 1865 to his friend William Verheyst, begging him to come at once, since something wonderful has happened.

Leopold, a poor gentleman who has barely kept out of debt by strict economy, has all at once come into an immense fortune. His mother's old aunt, unknown to him and quarrelled with all her relations, made him sole heir to all her property. A million, he writes, has been thrown at his head. The novel that follows turns on fortune, friendship, and its surprises.
28871-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
David Widger edited this linked index to George Rawlinson's Seven Great Monarchies of the Ancient Asian World, with his History of Phoenicia. Rawlinson, who lived from 1812 to 1902, treats Chaldaea, Assyria, Media, Babylon, Persia, Parthia, and the Sassanian Empire. Each monarchy gets chapters on country, climate, people, language, arts, manners, religion, and history.

The Chaldaea section alone lists plates of Mugheir ruins, Warka, cuneiform inscriptions, and a restored temple. The index lets a reader move through Rawlinson's vast survey monarchy by monarchy, with pictures and plans beside the text. Scholars and general readers get a guide to a classic Victorian history of the ancient Near East, still useful for its scope and illustrations.
29698-lighter-than-you-think:
Nelson Bond's short tale of Pat Pending, the greatest inventulator of all time, comes from Blue Book, which printed more than a dozen Pat Pending stories. Sandy beams at everyone, her eyes needing only jet propulsion to become flying saucers. Was Pat not wonderful? A joker of old won two-bit immortality by saying the nation wants a cheap cigar.

Bond answers with Victorian malarkey: the nation really wants a cheap nickel, or a cigar-shaped spaceship. A fortune waits among the stars for whoever can travel lighter than he thinks. Fans of Bond will enjoy a light, laughing tale of invention, with a federal employee of the Patent Office at its heart.
33606-the-fairy-school-of-castle-frank:
Grant Balfour writes a Canadian fairy tale for children in this 1899 Toronto book, recommended by Ontario's premier, G. W. Ross, as interesting, instructive, and morally useful. One hundred years before the telling, a boy named Robin lived in the grand old Canadian woods among wapitis, wolves, and bears. His wooden home was called Castle Frank, near a deep ravine and a slow river flowing into a great blue lake.

Eight chapters follow Romantic Robin into fairyland, a strange school class, advice from Hug-grippy the affectionate and from a subtle snake, a modest medallist, a fight in the ravine, and Robin's book. Balfour mixes woodland adventure with lessons in courage and kindness. Young readers will enjoy its Canadian setting and its gentle fairy-school fantasy.
34663-commodore-junk:
George Manville Fenn wrote a sea novel in an edition dated 1889, opening down in Devon. Captain Armstrong faces an angry young woman named Mary. Then you're a villain, she cries. He asks her to be reasonable, and she answers that she is reasonable and telling truth. Is it true, she demands, that he is to marry that lady?

He admits, haltingly, that he supposes he is. Fenn wrote dozens of adventure tales for boys and general readers. His sea stories mix romance ashore with peril afloat. The commodore of the title commands a vessel the nickname Junk makes comic. The opening quarrel sets the love plot against the sea plot.
36053-little-jack-rabbit-and-chippy-chip:
Little Jack Rabbit and Chippy Chipmunk, by David Cory, bears a copyright of 1921. Grosset and Dunlap issued the book in New York, with drawings by Barbour. Cory had written a shelf of Little Jack Rabbit books before this one.

The contents list reads like a year of small adventures: Lollypop Syrup, Doctor Heron, and the Song of Promise. The first tale opens as Little Jack hops home to the Old Bramble Patch. He finds a big tin pail half full of lollypop juice under a spout in a yellow lollypop tree. Other tales bring Granddaddy Bullfrog, Photographer Crane, and Doctor Quack. Chippy Chipmunk shows Jack his stock of nuts in a front picture. Bags of peanuts, a musical alarm clock, and Danny Fox fill out the set.
37423-how-we-think:
John Dewey, professor of philosophy at Columbia University, wrote a book on how we think, copyrighted in 1910 by D C Heath. Part one treats the problem of training thought. Chapter one asks what thought is. The need for training thought follows, then natural resources in the training. Dewey defines reflective thought as active, persistent, and careful consideration.

A complete act of thought, he argues, moves from a felt difficulty to testing a suggestion. Schools, he holds, must train this habit rather than stuff facts. The book became a classic of American education. Dewey later rewrote it in 1933. Teachers still assign its five phases of reflection.
38318-george-cruikshank:
W H Chesson wrote George Cruikshank for the Popular Library of Art, edited by Edward Garnett and issued at London by Duckworth. Front pages list mate volumes on Durer, Rossetti, Rembrandt, and Millet with their picture counts. Cruikshank stands in that list by Chesson. A front print shows George Cruikshank Frightening Society from his Omnibus of 1842.

Chesson had writ Name This Child. The series aimed to give short lives of great artists with many prints for plain readers. Fred Walker, Leonardo, Gainsborough, and Botticelli fill mate volumes in the list. Raphael and Velazquez are writ by Auguste Breal and Julia Cartwright in turn. The Cruikshank volume treats the famed caricaturist and book artist in that brief, pictured form. His humour and his long career in print are its theme.
38990-ovington-s-bank:
Stanley Weyman wrote this novel of Ovington's Bank and county town life. Longmans printed it in New York in the year 1922. Weyman past tales fill a long list, The Castle Inn among them. Forty two chapters carry the bank tale to its close.

Chapter one opens on market day at Aldersbury, Aldshire old town. Saint Juliana clock nears three as streets throng with folk. Gentry head homeward while a carriage and four waits at post. A red wheeled tandem cart stands near with keen horses. Under the Red Robe and Count Hannibal stand among his famed earlier works listed.
39110-phil-may-s-gutter-snipes-50-origin:
Phil May Gutter Snipes is a book of fifty pen and ink sketches. The Leadenhall Press of London issued this proof edition in a limited run. Only one thousand fifty copies were printed on fine paper as proofs. This copy is numbered four hundred sixty two in that set.

A list of drawings names Grace as frontispiece, then Shuttlecock and a Gutter Ball. Playing at Soldiers, Water Works, and a Game at Ball follow in turn. Longing for Lickings, Luxuries, Plunderers, Lost, and Homeless show the street child theme. The Slide, the First Smoke, and Brother Artists fill the middle plates. May draws London gutter children at play with wit and pity.
40253-peachmonk:
John Eyerman wrote Peachmonk, a serio comic detective tale in which no firearms are used and no one is killed, issued in New York in nineteen seventeen. The tale is a three days episode in the life of the Duke of Belleville, as related by Lord Edward Lyndon. Its fabric rests on book titles, about nine hundred woven into the prose in capitals.

No literary merit is claimed for the tale, as none has been attempted, Eyerman warns. A letter from Barchester Towers, Kenilworth, opens the frame. The writer asks Eyerman to finish a tale left undone when Scarlett was ordered to India. Titles like Our Mutual Friend and Far from the Madding Crowd stud each sentence. Word game fans get a puzzle novel built from a library shelf.
45951-monk:
Julian Corbett wrote Monk for the English Men of Action series, printed in London in 1889. George Monk rose from Devon service abroad to high command in war at home. Corbett traces how Monk served king and then Parliament in turn.

Chapters cover the treaty with Irish forces, service under Cromwell, and command at sea. Later parts show Monk as governor of Scotland and as the man who helped bring back the king in a bloodless shift of power. Corbett calls him a father of his country. Readers get a clear life of a key figure in a time of civil war.
50753-later-than-you-think:
Fritz Leiber wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in October 1950. Far in the future, an Explorer comes back to the study of an Archeologist friend. The room glows with soft light from its walls. Books bound in metal line the shelves, and a bright fish hangs in mid-air.

The two friends talk in a tongue far from any speech we know. The Explorer asks what the search has found, and the talk turns on how late the hour truly is. Leiber builds the whole tale on mood and one stark thought. The green light and sea-dark art make the far age feel real and strange.
53034-the-god-plllnk:
The God Plllnk is a tale of Mars visitors by Jerome Bixby. It first ran in a fiction magazine in December of nineteen sixty three. A front plea warns star men to mind how they look on Mars. Two priests of Mars wait in a crater shade for their God to land.

The pair have crept and oozed all night to the place of the Gods fall. One is a high priest, the next a priest of yet more high rank. Mars hangs red in the black sky as the great Seeing Eye of their God. Their whole folk have sent good will with them on the grave task. What lands will test their faith in a sharp, droll turn.
57619-striped-coat-the-skunk:
Joseph Wharton Lippincott's Striped Coat, the Skunk, illustrated by the author, was published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1922. Lippincott had already written Bun, a Wild Rabbit, Red Ben, the Fox of Oak Ridge, and Gray Squirrel.

The contents follow the wood pussy's life: his journey, strong medicine, the brush pile, the burning woods, and good hunting. Later chapters promise fifty dollars on his head, capture at last, the winter sleep, the spring awakening, and raising a family, ending with Master of the Woods. The first chapter opens under a full moon over the narrow waters of Goose Creek. Light slips between the cedars, pines, and oaks onto the sand and the carpet of dead leaves.
57950-the-grey-monk:
T W Speight, author of The Mysteries of Heron Dyke, wrote a novel published in London in 1894. Chapter heads open with Alec's sentence and an old family and its home. An offer and its acceptance lead to a blow at one stroke. The ebony casket enters at chapter eight.

Ethel and Tamsin, Launce Keymer, and a recreant lover people the middle. Captain Verinder takes a little journey. Three conspirators plot, and Sir Gilbert hears the news. A false heir is named, and Luigi is acknowledged. Later chapters promise a deed of darkness and the defeat of roguery. The root of the mystery is promised at chapter forty three of forty nine.
59146-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of George Cruikshank works on Gutenberg. Four Hundred Humorous Illustrations heads the list of the set. The Bachelor Own Book and the Centenary Garland follow in order. Points of Humour parts one and two stand in the contents.

Pamphlets and parodies on political subjects and Jack Sheppard follow next. Cruikshank water colours, Saint Dunstan legend, and Lord Bateman ballad appear. Oliver Twist, Joseph Grimaldi memoirs, and Punch and Judy stand listed. Tables of contents for the volumes follow the master list here. The Tower of London and the Comic Almanack volumes stand near the end of the list.
60893-thinking-and-learning-to-think:
Thinking and Learning to Think, a treatise on education by Nathan C Schaeffer, was published by J B Lippincott Company of Philadelphia in 1906. It stands first in Lippincott's Educational Series, edited by Martin G Brumbaugh. Schaeffer was Superintendent of Public Instruction for the state of Pennsylvania. The book runs to three hundred fifty one pages.

The editor's preface hails a great awakening in the training of teachers. Professional schools, city training schools, and university departments of pedagogy were rising on every hand. Leading posts in schools and supervision, he says, now demand trained leaders. That demand calls for standard treatises on the fundamental problems of education. Schaeffer's subject is the act of thought itself: how minds think, and how schools can teach them to think better.
61990-a-sermon-preach-d-upon-the-occasio:
A Sermon is a church talk by Nathanael Hough, a fellow of a great hall at Cambridge. It was spoke at the church of a town near the court on a feast day of seventeen hundred and six. That day is kept each year for the fifth of the eleventh month. The talk was print at London in seventeen hundred and seven. It is sworn to the men and folk of that town.

This is the next such piece of my work made known past such a day, the sworn leaf says. None can be more glad at the two fold bless of the day than you, it goes on. You are the best folk of the queen, and the most near kin to her court as well.
65308-billy-mink:
Billy Mink is a beast tale for the young by Thornton Burgess, with drawn plates by Harrison Cady. Its first rights date is nineteen nineteen. It is one of a set of tales of one pool and its beast folk, in a chain of such sets by Burgess. The front lists name his past sets on the meadow, the wood, and the wind mother.

Parts trace Billy as he sniffs a trap, beats the trap man, and finds strange fences. He warns his friend the coon, and the two put their heads as one. Late parts take the pair to a great barn where rats plot to kill Billy. A sign of risk, a fail of the rats plot, and a flight of the rats fill the close of the list. Plain talk and short parts suit new readers.
68991-giant-brains-or-machines-that-thin:
Edmund Callis Berkeley introduces the first electronic computers to general readers in this 1949 book from John Wiley of New York and Chapman and Hall of London. He calls the new machines giant brains, or machines that think. They handle information with great skill and great speed, he says, a brain-like power. They do the work of hundreds for the wages of a dozen, and stand beside atomic energy among the century's great achievements.

His first chapter argues the question whether a machine can think. The book then examines several machines in the order they were finished between 1942 and 1946. They are the differential analyzer from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard's IBM automatic sequence-controlled calculator, the Moore School's ENIAC, and the Bell Laboratories relay calculator. Berkeley closes by judging what such machines will do in the future.
68996-angel-a-sketch-in-indian-ink:
Angel is a sketch in Indian ink by Croker, printed at New York in 1901. Croker also wrote Beyond the Pale and Infatuation. Dodd, Mead issued the book, and Croker dedicates it to Perrin. Forty chapters carry the tale, from Patience on a Gate to In Garhwal and beyond.

A verse at the front calls woman a foreign land whose customs a man never quite understands. The tale opens in mid-March in the North-West Provinces, where the hot weather sends its heralds to Ramghur. Punkahs swing lazily in the barrack rooms. Families quit the sweltering cantonments for the hills. Croker sets her love story in an Anglo-Indian station at the edge of summer.
70163-millbank:
Mary J Holmes wrote Millbank, or Roger Irving's Ward, a novel entered for rights in eighteen seventy-one. Holmes was known for Tempest and Sunshine, Lena Rivers, and English Orphans. The publisher's list calls her a pleasant writer who holds her readers fast.

The contents promise a stranger in Belvidere, a stir at Millbank, and Frank at Millbank. Roger's letters bring a result, and a loose board in the garret hides something. Later chapters turn to love-making at Millbank and the start of trouble. Holmes gave the story to her publisher, George W Carleton, as a friend. Brockport, New York, is the dateline.
70211-at-hotel-on-de-blink:
At Hotel On de Blink is a stage entertainment in two parts by George P Seiler, printed at Boston by Walter H Baker and Company in 1916. Seiler had also written Schmerecase in School. The piece is a dialect comedy set in a cheap hotel.

The cast holds Hans Seitz, who owns the place, and his daughter Gretch. A knight of the road named Samp L Case checks in, with a lost Italian guest and a bell hop called the wise kid. Signs in the lobby joke on prices, with tripe at five cents a yard and board at five cents a foot. Costume notes call for a suit much too large and Dutch chin whiskers for Hans. Player groups get a short, broad farce full of thick accents.
71239-the-bobbsey-twins-at-cloverbank:
The Bobbsey Twins at Cloverbank is a children's novel by Laura Lee Hope, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1926. It is one of the long Bobbsey Twins series, named on the title page with Hope's other runs. The frontispiece shows a child crying out at a paddle wheel in full turn. The contents promise a country holiday with a puzzle in it. A mysterious box opens the tale. Queer noises follow, then an invitation and a prize offer.

Off for Cloverbank takes the twins to their holiday place at last. A lonely cabin and a night camp stand in the mid chapters. The Bobbsey twins, two sets of brother and sister, were the stock heroes of the series. Their tales mix small perils with safe ends for young readers. Cloverbank gives them a farm stay with a secret to solve.
73104-israel-rank:
Israel Rank, by Roy Horniman, calls itself the autobiography of a criminal. A first note tests the old saying that murder will out. The narrator doubts that claim and calls it a mere matter of opinion. Clumsy criminals in full view of the law prove little, he argues.

Rank holds that many a liked member of society has removed a human block. Such a man, he says, acted with no pang of conscience at all. Chapter one then opens on a bleak autumn day in Clapham. Dust and leaves whirl through shabby streets of small semi detached villas. That grim set scene launches a cool and dark crime tale.
73536-the-kink:
The Kink, by Thomson Burtis, is a flying story headed, When an Airman Grows Too Old to Fly. It opens in the flying office at McCook Field. Finley strides to the desk of the operations clerk and asks, with a sunny Irish smile, what old hulk he must haul round the field that day.

The old sergeant, ill at ease, gives him the Larkin. Finley explodes: for a month he has had only crates fit for a museum. Then young Kink Forell laughs from above, in helmet and coveralls, parachute under his arm. He mocks Finley as the official scavenger of ships for the field. Readers get a tale of airmen, pride, and old planes, built on the clash between a fading flyer and a radiant young one.
75018-the-curse-of-drink:
W C Tuttle, writer of western tales, sets a comic story in the cowtown of San Pablo, told by Hozie Sykes in his own loose drawl.

Hozie and his partner Peewee Parker agree to act in a play. The show is staged for the benefit of Parson Jones. Peewee weighs two hundred and fifty pounds on the hoof. The cast of the town includes Hank Potts, six feet six and thin as a rifle, who runs the No-Limit Saloon and the HP cow outfit. The headnote warns that when the last curtain falls, among other things, the chief winner of the riot will be Eveline Annabel Wimple. Tuttle's humour runs on tall talk and pride knocked flat, and this tale gives his stock pair a stage, a crowd, and liquor enough to wreck both.
76921-what-to-drink:
What to Drink, by Bertha Stockbridge, was published in New York and London in 1920 as a blue book of drinks without alcohol. Stockbridge, author of The Liberty Cook Book, gives recipes and serving directions for all sorts of events. A short verse at the front jokes that lemonade can make Prohibition feel like paradise.

Chapters cover fruit drinks, punches, alcohol-free mixed drinks, syrups, grape juice, and milk drinks. Later sections treat coffee, tea, drinks for sick people and small children, sundaes, sauces, and ices. Stockbridge opens with a firm rule about care in measuring. Exact cups and spoons, she says, are what make a drink come out right every time.
77418-the-history-of-drink:
James Samuelson, a barrister of the Middle Temple, wrote The History of Drink, published in London in 1878. He calls it a review of drink in social, scientific, and political terms. The book is dedicated, with leave, to Sir John Lubbock, a noted man of science.

In his preface Samuelson notes that writers of every age had treated drinking, yet few had covered the whole subject in a planned way. He praises an older treatise by Samuel Morewood, printed in 1824, as a store of curious facts on the drinks of all times and nations. His own work aims to bring that wide story up to date. Readers get brewing, custom, law, and temperance argued in one volume.
79649-a-minute-to-think:
Ray Humphreys wrote this Western tale, A Minute to Think. Humphreys also wrote Crazy on Birds. It opens on a bright morning in Gunsight that one man cannot enjoy. Old Pappy Stewart, senior driver for the Q-B Stage Lines, stands silent in the doorway of the big barn, hands deep in his pockets, while the younger hands chaff him.

His eyes are fixed on the cause: a brand new motor bus, red and yellow, its motor purring like a cat in the stage yard. Pappy's whip is gone, and his driving gauntlets are tucked under his arm. The company means to replace its two six-mule stages with buses, and to make a bus driver of Pappy. Pappy, half mule himself for stubbornness, has balked, and his first question is for his six black mules.
8430-the-mountebank:
William J. Locke's novel opens in June 1919, when the narrator receives a long letter from Brigadier-General Andrew Lackaday, sent from an obscure hotel in Marseilles, with a bulky manuscript. Lackaday kept his friend up till morning with his story, and the manuscript that follows tells it: the life of a mountebank, a showman and wanderer, in Locke's warm, romantic style.

Locke, a popular novelist of the Edwardian years, writes of outsiders with sympathy, and Lackaday's tale moves between war, show business, and love. Readers get a framed narrative, a letter opening a life, in the tradition of stories told by friends. The novel's charm lies in its hero, a performer who lives by his wits and his heart.
9462-the-tale-of-sandy-chipmunk:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote The Tale of Sandy Chipmunk in 1916, a children's animal tale from his Sleepy-Time series. Sandy, a young chipmunk, gets his name, builds a house, and learns the ways of field and farm. Harry L. Smith drew the pictures, which show Sandy's mishaps in bright scenes. The book speaks in short, plain words for small readers.

Chapters follow a broken egg, samples of wheat, a store kept by Uncle Sammy, and work for Mr. Crow. Sandy gets a letter, rides to the miller's, and plants corn in his turn. A reader gets a gentle woodland tale of work, friends, and growing up, told with humor and a fond eye for small beasts.
949-tom-swift-and-his-submarine-boat-or-:
Tom Swift builds a submarine boat in this adventure by Victor Appleton, and he sails under the ocean for sunken treasure. News of a treasure wreck starts the tale, and Mr. Berg, a rival, grows astonished, then suspicious, as Tom finishes his craft. Tom is even imprisoned before he turns the tables.

Mr. Damon joins the voyage, Captain Weston aids the search, and the sea yields perils and prizes in turn. Appleton writes with brisk, boyish energy, mixing invention with adventure. The book is a classic Tom Swift tale, where a young inventor's machine opens a hidden world beneath the waves.
britannica-1911-bank:
Bank, also called Polish Bank or Russian Bank, is a card game played with an ordinary pack. Five or six players make a convenient number. Each puts an agreed stake into a pool. The dealer gives three cards to every player and turns up one more. He goes on dealing until a card no higher than an eight shows, with ace counting lowest.

The player at the dealer's left bets, without touching or even looking at his own cards, that among them sits a higher card of the same suit as the turn-up. He may bet the whole pool or any part of it. Winners take their sum from the pool; losers pay in. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the round's order, the fresh stakes when the pool empties, and the fine for touching cards early.
britannica-1911-blank:
Blank is a word study drawn from the French blanc, meaning white. The core sense is something left white, waiting to be filled in. The entry works through the chief uses of the word in law, money, trade, and games, one by one.

A blank cheque still needs its amount written in, and a policy in blank lacks the name of the person it pays. Blank verse is verse without rhyme, and a blank cartridge holds powder but no ball or shot. As a noun, a blank can be a losing lottery ticket with no number on it. It can also be the plain metal disc, not yet stamped, from which a coin is made.
britannica-1911-chesil-bank:
Chesil Bank is a remarkable beach of shingle on the coast of Dorsetshire, England, its name taken from an Anglo-Saxon word for a pebble bank. An inlet called the Fleet, famous for its swannery, divides the bank from the mainland for eight miles. In all the bank runs 18 miles south-eastward from Abbotsbury. It ends at the so-called Isle of Portland, where it stands highest above the tide.

At the Portland end the bank rises 35 feet above spring tide level and spreads 200 yards wide. Height falls toward the west, where the breadth is only 170 yards. Pebble size falls with it, from one to three inches across at Portland to the size of peas at the western end. The entry ties both changes to shingle moving along this coast from west to east.
britannica-1911-clydebank:
Clydebank is a police burgh of Dumbartonshire, Scotland, on the right bank of the Clyde six miles from Glasgow, with 21,591 people in 1901. Stations at Yoker, Clydebank, Kilbowie and Dalmuir, all within the burgh since 1886, are served by the North British and Caledonian railways. In 1875 the district was almost purely rural. Since that date flourishing industries have been planted in its different parts, transforming it within a generation.

Large shipbuilding yards and engineering works stand at Clydebank itself, with some shipbuilding and a distillery at Yoker. At Kilbowie the Singer Manufacturing Company has an immense factory covering nearly 50 acres and employing many thousands of operatives. Dalmuir holds the building and repairing yards of the Clyde Navigation Trust, whose Rothesay Dock opened in April 1907. The municipality owns a fine town hall and buildings, and part of the parish crosses the Clyde into Renfrewshire.
britannica-1911-george-the-monk:
George the Monk, a Byzantine chronicler, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was also called Hamartolos, a Greek word for sinner. He lived in the reign of Michael the Third, from 842 to 867. He wrote a Chronicle of events in four books.

The Chronicle runs from the creation of the world to the death of the emperor Theophilus, in 842. In that same year, the widow Theodora restored the worship of images. For the years 813 to 842, his work is the only original source from the time itself. That makes it, so far, indispensable, the text says. The early parts are merely a compilation. In his opening, the author disclaims all claims to literary style. His sole aim, he declares, was to relate things useful and necessary, with strict adherence to truth. The article adds that far too much space goes to other matter.
britannica-1911-gilbert-sir-william-schw:
Sir William Schwenk Gilbert (1836- ) is an English playwright and humorist, born in London on 18 November 1836. The 1911 Britannica entry makes his father, also William Gilbert, a novelist whose books the son illustrated, showing an early gift for whimsical drawing. The younger Gilbert was educated at Boulogne, Ealing and King's College, taking his degree in 1856.

A hoped-for artillery commission died with the Crimean War's end. He worked in the privy council's education office, then was called to the bar in 1864, with a small practice. From 1861 he wrote for the comic journal Fun, and his Bab Ballads grew from that work. The entry goes on to his stage career and his famous run of Savoy operas with Sullivan, naming pieces such as H.M.S. Pinafore and Patience. A Middlesex magistracy of 1891 satisfied his old legal ambition.
britannica-1911-greenshank:
Greenshank is the subject of a bird article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The greenshank is one of the largest birds in the sandpiper group. Its legs are a dull olive colour, which hardly fits its English name. That name, the text says, was meant to set it apart from two kin birds with red legs. Those kin are called redshanks.

The article describes a slim bird with long legs and neck, near a woodcock in bulk. It is native to the north of the Old World. In winter it wanders far south, to Africa, India, and Australia. Disturbed from moor or marsh, it rises fast with shrill cries and shows a white back. It breeds in the Hebrides and the Scottish Highlands. It also breeds across northern Europe and Asia. Two like species in North America are named at the end.
britannica-1911-holl-frank:
Frank Holl (1845–1888) was an English painter, born in London on the 4th of July 1845. He was the grandson of William Holl, an engraver of note, and son of Francis Holl, another engraver, whose trade he first meant to follow. He entered the Royal Academy schools in 1860, won silver and gold medals, and first exhibited in 1864. Pictures such as Convalescent and Faces in the Fire followed fast.

Holl won the travelling studentship in 1868 with The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away, a picture that made a furore. Its blackness of colour, blamed on his engraver's training, counted against it, as did its sadness. Still, it showed his best gifts: strong technique and a sincere vein of pathos. His range was narrow, and his portraits stand well below Millais. A mania for work of all kinds began early to wreck his health.
britannica-1911-ink:
Ink, a substance for making marks and writing on paper, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term for the purple ink used by Greek and Roman emperors. In its widest sense it covers two kinds of colour matter. One is fluid writing ink for pen or brush, and the other is the thick printing ink used with type and plates.

The ancient Egyptians made and used inks, and a written papyrus survives from about 2500 before Christ. In China the invention is ascribed to Tien Tcheu, of an age still earlier. Early inks were made from charcoal or soot mixed with gum, glue, or varnish. Sepia, the black fluid of the cuttlefish, served the Romans as a writing fluid. Iron gall ink, from an iron salt and tannin, came into common use in later centuries.
britannica-1911-ladybank:
Ladybank is a police burgh of Fifeshire, Scotland, 5½ m. S.W. of Cupar by the North British railway and ½ m. from the left bank of the Eden. Its population in 1901 was 1340. Besides standing on the main line to Dundee, it connects with Perth and Kinross, and it is a railway junction of some importance with a locomotive depot. Its industries are linen weaving, coal mining and malting.

Kettle, a village 1 m. S., has prehistoric barrows and a fort, and Collessie has a standing stone and traces of ancient camps. The boundary between Collessie and Monimail parishes runs in a crescent called the Bow of Fife. In Monimail stands the Mount, once the home of the poet Sir David Lindsay, and a Doric pillar 100 ft. high raised to John Hope, 4th earl of Hopetoun.
britannica-1911-lockwood-sir-frank:
Sir Frank Lockwood (1846-1897) was an English lawyer of Doncaster stock. His grandfather and great-grandfather had both been mayors of the town. A private school, Manchester grammar school, and Caius College, Cambridge, formed him. The bar at Lincoln's Inn called him in 1872.

Fees rose fast: 120 guineas in year one, 265 in year two. Queen's counsel came in 1882. Recorder of Sheffield came in 1884. York sent him to parliament as a Liberal in 1885, after two failed bids. Solicitor-general under Rosebery came in 1894, with a knighthood. The post lasted less than a year. A trip to the American Bar meeting in 1896 won praise for his wit at table. He died in London on 18 December 1897. Pen-and-ink caricatures, a gift from his father, filled his spare hours.
britannica-1911-mauch-chunk:
Mauch Chunk is a borough in Pennsylvania, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica maps it in a full gazetteer entry. The borough is the county seat of Carbon county. It stands on the west bank of the Lehigh river, along the Lehigh Coal and Navigation Company canal. Its count was 4,029 in 1900 and 3,952 in 1910.

The entry shows a town squeezed by steep ground. One street runs along the river, and the main street cuts through a deep side valley. A ward called Upper Mauch Chunk sits high on the hill above. An incline railway, first built to haul coal down to the river, now carries tourists up Mount Pisgah and Mount Jefferson. Coal mining, silk, and stove making support the town.
britannica-1911-pink:
Pink, in botany, is the common name for a genus of plants, and this 1911 Britannica entry sets out the marks of the group. The botanists' name for it is Dianthus. Its plants bear simple leaves in pairs at the thickened joints of the stem. The flowers end the stem and have a tube-shaped calyx ringed by overlapping scales, a showy crown of five free petals on long stalks, and ten stamens.

The seed vessel ripens into a one-chambered pod holding many seeds, opening at the top by four teeth. The species are low perennial herbs, often with very showy flowers. They grow wild chiefly in southern Europe and around the Mediterranean, with a few in temperate Asia and South Africa. Four species are wild in Britain, among them the Deptford pink and the maiden pink.
britannica-1911-rutley-frank:
Frank Rutley, an English geologist who lived from 1842 to 1904, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Dover on May 14, 1842. His love of earth science was lit at the Royal School of Mines. He served as an army officer till 1867, then joined the Geological Survey.

In the Lake District Rutley took up the close study of rocks and their parts. He became the survey's rock expert at its London museum. His books list a text on minerals, The Study of Rocks, and works on granite and green stone. He wrote site reports on the rocks of Somerset, Brent Tor, and Wales. From 1882 he taught at the Royal College of Science.
britannica-1911-stone-frank:
Frank Stone, a British painter who lived from 1800 to 1859, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born in Manchester. He was entirely self-taught as an artist. In 1833 he was elected an associate of the Society of Painters in Water Colours. He became a full member in 1843.

In 1851 he was made an associate of the Royal Academy. The works he first showed at the Academy were portraits. From 1840 onward he sent figure pictures instead. His themes came from Shakespeare, from scripture, and from sentimental tales. Many of his works were engraved for wider sale. The article gives a short record of a painter who rose with no master to teach him. His path ran from portraits to the story scenes the public of his day loved best.
britannica-1911-tonk:
Tonk is a native state of India in the Rajputana agency, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes its odd make-up. The state consists of six separate tracts, some of them lying under the Central India agency. Its whole area comes to 2,553 square miles and its people to 273,201 in 1901. No tribute is payable. Its chief, who bears the title of nawab, is a Muslim of Afghan descent.

The founder of the family was Amir Khan, the famed Pindari leader, who received the land when he submitted to the British in 1817. The nawab of 1911 succeeded in 1867 and attended two great durbars as a ruling chief. The town of Tonk stands sixty miles south of Jaipur and held 38,759 people in 1901.
britannica-1911-ward-lester-frank:
Lester Frank Ward, an American geologist and sociologist born in 1841, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Joliet in Illinois, he left Columbian University in 1869 and its law school in 1871. His studies had been held up by service in the Union army in the Civil War. He worked at the Treasury till 1872, then joined the Geological Survey, rising to geologist in 1888.

Ward wrote much on fossil plants, with books on their spread and on the plant life of the Mesozoic age. He taught botany at Columbian for two years as well. His wider fame rests on sociology. There he reshaped the thought of Herbert Spencer and fought Spencer's stress on the lone person. He set social facts beside mind and matter as one chain. His chief books run from Dynamic Sociology of 1883 to Pure Sociology of 1903.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-paula-v:
Franz Paula von Schrank, born at Varnbach near Scharding on the Inn on 21 August 1747 and died at Munich on 22 December 1835, was a German Jesuit naturalist and botanist.

After the suppression he was ordained priest at Vienna in December 1774, took a theology doctorate in 1776, and published his first natural history contributions. He taught mathematics and physics at Amberg and rhetoric at Burghausen, studying agriculture there, and in 1784 became professor of agriculture, mining, forestry, botany, and zoology at Ingolstadt University, later Landshut. In 1809 the Munich Academy made him director of its new botanical garden, his life's work thereafter. His writings fill nine columns in the Jesuit bibliography, closing with scriptural works on the six days of creation and a literal commentary on Genesis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-xaver-v:
Franz Xaver von Funk, born at Abtsgmund in Wurttemberg on 12 October 1840 and died at Tubingen on 24 February 1907, was a German church historian whose critical method founded a school. Son of an innkeeper, he attended Ellwangen gymnasium and entered Tubingen University in 1859. He lived at the Wilhelmsstift, studied philosophy and theology with ancient philology and political economy. He won the political science faculty prize of 1862 for an essay on what police meant in the eighteenth century.

 Back in 1866, he became tutor at the Wilhelmsstift, guiding students' personal studies. He rose to Tubingen's church history chair, where his sole aim, seeking historical truth, frank and honest character, and severity toward opponents swayed by other motives created a school. It advanced earnest, scholarly criticism among German Catholic historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-sigis:
Michael Sigismund Frank, a Catholic artist and rediscoverer of the lost art of glass painting, was born at Nuremberg on 1 June 1770 and died at Munich on 16 January 1847. His father, a well-off provisions dealer, meant him for the business, but the boy's passion for art thwarted the plan. His mother, unknown to her husband, had him taught drawing at the local academy, where his progress astonished friends.

Orphaned young, Frank was apprenticed to his godfather Neubert, who lacquered and decorated wooden boxes and caskets at Nuremberg. Back with his remarried mother, he studied drawing again, painting boxes for other makers to pay his way. At twenty-one his parents pressed him, against his will, to wed Marie Blechkoll, whose dowry brought the inn Zur Himmelsleiter. Frank was no innkeeper: while his wife ran the hotel, he kept studying art and turned to porcelain painting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monk:
A monk is a man living in community apart from the world. He lives under vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, following the rule of his particular order. The word itself is popular rather than official church language. Its English form comes through Anglo-Saxon munuc from Latin monachus, a borrowing of Greek monachos. That Greek root ties to ideas of solitude and unity.

Early church fathers already disagreed about the root. Jerome stressed the solitary, while Augustine stressed the oneness of brethren living as one. The entry traces the word's history. It separates monks proper from friars and canons. It notes how the solitary hermit gave way to community life under a rule, with the great orders of East and West shaping what monkhood became.
doe-osti-2589593-probabilistic-error-bou:
Error bars on a workhorse of big data analysis are the product of Sandia final report SAND2025-11681R, by Daniel Dunlavy, Richard Lehoucq, Carlos Llosa-Vite, and co-authors. Low-rank tensor decompositions compress multi-way data, such as measurements indexed by time, place, and type, into small summaries. Users need to know how much of the original data a summary might miss.

The team derived probability-based error bounds for these compressions. A key step reduced the tensor problem to a matrix sketching problem, which unlocked both new algorithms and proofs of their limits. Results give near-best-possible sample counts for completing a rank-1 tensor from partial entries, meaning filling a sparse grid from few samples. Higher-rank cases remain open, and the report charts that path for data scientists.
doe-osti-3021931-evaluation-of-hanford-2:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Brett C. Simpson, Reid A. Peterson, and Amy M. Westesen, dated August 2025, evaluates what is physically inside Hanford's 200 West Area tank farms. The 241-S, 241-SX, and 241-U farms hold sludge and saltcake from decades of plutonium production. A planned West Area Tank Treatment process must pump, dissolve, and treat that waste, and its design depends on physical properties: densities, settling, and dissolution behavior by waste type.

The assessment separates the waste into families with distinct behavior. Boehmite-rich sludges came from REDOX process waste that boiled; gibbsite-rich sludges came from cladding waste; saltcakes show lower aluminum-to-chromium ratios and dissolve differently. Tanks S-110 and S-111 hold the largest anticipated volumes of insoluble solids. Where a waste type lacked tests, results from similar West Area saltcakes stood in, a gap the report flags.
george-cruikshank:
William Makepeace Thackeray praised the caricaturist George Cruikshank in this essay from the Westminster Review of June 1840. Thackeray opens with a meditation on ingratitude, lost youth, and the fog of adult striving, then turns to the artist whose drawings had delighted that youth. Cruikshank illustrated fairy tales, Dickens, and the drunkard's progress of popular prints, and Thackeray knew the work as a fellow pen-and-pencil man.

The essay mixes memoir, criticism, and gratitude, urging a busy world to honor the humorist who stocked its imagination. Thackeray writes of Cruikshank's grotesques, his temperance plates, and his fairy grotesquerie with a cartoonist's professional love. It is one Victorian artist's tribute to another, and a small classic of appreciative criticism.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIATerpilFrank_:
Frank Terpil had been a CIA contract man before he became an international arms dealer, and the Washington Post's Arms Agent With Hazardous Habit catches him at the fall. Terpil was arrested for trying to sell 10,000 machine guns to men who turned out to be undercover detectives.

Together with Edwin Wilson, Terpil became the emblem of the ex-agent gone rogue: agency training and contacts turned to private gunrunning for dictators and middlemen. His later flight from American justice completed the legend. The article is preserved as the newspaper's account of the arrest that started his downfall.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DonnerFrank_Don:
The December 1, 1984 issue of The Nation magazine carries an article by Harrison E. Salisbury with an unlikely subject. Its title is The Strange Correspondence of Morris Ernst and John Edgar Hoover, 1939-1964. Ernst was a famed civil liberties lawyer; Hoover ran the FBI. Their letters ran for twenty-five years.

Salisbury's piece examines what passed between a man who defended free speech and the director who kept files on dissenters. The friendship puzzled both men's reputations. The issue preserves the article as readers first met it, inside a leading journal of the American left.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WrightFrank_Wri: A letter dated June 30, 1968, went to Frank Wright of the Freedom Institute. The writer's name is not recorded in the record. Letters to small political and educational groups filled many research files of the period. The Wright letter is one surviving piece of that traffic, written while debate over the Warren Report and the King and Robert Kennedy killings was at full heat.
podcast-dannyjones-TAzeJl8n4nk:
Jimmy Corsetti, who researches ancient mysteries online, and Dan Richards join Danny Jones for a crowded hour. One subject is a new controversy over Gobekli Tepe's excavation and future. The other is the earth's next magnetic pole flip. The guests discuss the flip as a coming event with ancient precedents.

Corsetti has fought publicly with archaeologists over access and interpretation at the Turkish site, and he states that fight here. The pole flip thread adds geophysics to archaeology, two slow sciences asked to deliver sudden drama. The guests' readings are their own, contested by both fields they borrow from. The episode preserves the current state of alternative archaeology's two favorite live stories, argued by the men driving them, in the room where their audiences actually gather.
podcast-joerogan-QCJUEqppqNk:
Author Douglas Murray talks with Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, about people's need for religion. Murray, a British writer on culture and politics, argues that the hunger for the sacred does not die when churches empty. It moves somewhere else.

He traces where that hunger goes: into politics, identity, and new moral codes that act like faiths. Rogan asks whether anything can fill the gap without the old harms of dogma. The segment is a compact statement of Murray's case for the sacred, made in conversation rather than in print, and open to pushback.
podcast-joerogan-fds6Nm1QQNk:
Playwright David Mamet talks with Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, about the mythology of the Bible. Mamet, one of America's great dramatists, is also a sharp and cranky reader of scripture. His take honors the book's stories while refusing easy piety.

He argues that the Bible's tales carry the deep patterns of human life, which is why they still grip readers who share none of the faith. Rogan asks how a playwright reads characters like Abraham and Moses. The segment is a writer's tour of the good book, brisk, funny, and serious about story above all.
podcast-tuckercarlson-vUFtmvlOANk:
A journalist who lived in Israel for ten years joins Tucker Carlson to revisit October 7. Carlson says American news filters hide too much of the story. He calls the attack the start of a global shift.

The guest argues that a full timeline is needed to grasp that day. The title charges that Israel's leader funded Hamas for years. They discuss foreknowledge, dead Palestinians, and political gain. The talk is grave and detailed. It will draw listeners who want a critical account that American outlets rarely give in full. The claims are grave and fully aired.
the-missing-link:
Edward Dyson's 1922 novel The Missing Link opens with Dr. Crips's Healing Mixture, its first chapter. Nicholas Crips, called Nickie the Kid by his familiars, earns the nickname from kidder, a term for a smooth, flattering schemer with hidden motives. Even among companions expert in pretence, Nickie stood out as a specialist.

Crips is a thin, bony man of about five feet nine, often unshaven, whose worn black suit and moth-eaten cap suit his trade. Spareness helped him plead chronic sickness at back doors. When the chapter opens he is calling on housewives, retailing what hospital doctors supposedly said about his interesting heart weakness. His circle, the narrator explains, sat on the rail between honest work and open crime.
the-mountebank:
William J. Locke's novel The Mountebank begins in June 1919, when its narrator receives a long letter and a bulky manuscript from Brigadier-General Andrew Lackaday. The letter comes from an obscure hotel in Marseilles. Lackaday recounts how the narrator once listened all night to his wretched affairs and suggested he write a book about himself.

Lackaday protests that a layman cannot manage coherent narrative, and that English is nearly a foreign language to him, since he has thought all his life in French. Even the letter's prelude cost him two cigarettes. Instead he sends raw material from memory and diary: 673 sprawling foolscap pages covering his life, which, astonishingly, cut out the war years entirely, as the narrator marvels.
the-tale-of-sandy-chipmunk: Sandy Chipmunk, dated 1916, is one of Arthur Scott Bailey's Sleepy-Time Tales, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Title page and contents are what this record offers, and Sandy's adventures stop before they start. Fourteen listed chapters cover a broken egg, house building, samples of wheat, a basket of corn, work for Mr. Crow, and a ride to the miller's. One picture caption shows Sandy so startled that he dropped the eggs. The outline promises a small, busy chipmunk learning farmyard lessons the hard way.
tom-swift-and-his-submarine-boat-or-unde:
Victor Appleton opens his submarine story with a rushing, throbbing noise as a great body like an immense bird sails overhead, casting a grotesque shadow. An elderly man on a porch starts up in alarm. Contents promise twenty-five chapters, beginning with news of a treasure wreck and finishing the submarine.

Mr. Berg is astonished and suspicious, Tom is imprisoned, and tables turn before a trial dive. Later headings bring the ocean bed, diving suits, a tropical island race, sharks, and ramming the wreck. Readers get an underwater treasure adventure where the new boat is tested against rivals and the sea.
